seoTitle: Truck Accident Lawyer in Dearborn Heights, MI: Telegraph and Michigan Avenue, Ford Road and Warren Deliveries, the Federal Trucking Rules, a Carrier’s Safety Record, and the Evidence That Expires
seoDescription: Hit by a semi, box truck, or delivery truck in Dearborn Heights? 3,916 heavy trucks and buses were involved in Wayne County crashes in 2024. Learn how the federal trucking rules, the carrier’s $750,000-plus insurance, underride guards, and Michigan no-fault apply to a crash on Telegraph, Michigan Avenue, Ford Road, or Warren, how to check a carrier’s safety record, which agency owns the road, and why the logs must be preserved within days. h1: Dearborn Heights, MI Truck Accident Lawyer
tagline: Trucks run through both halves of Dearborn Heights on Telegraph, cross it on Michigan Avenue, and stop on Ford Road and Warren to supply its stores and restaurants. When a truck causes a crash here, the carrier, the trailer’s owner, and sometimes the shipper or the business it was serving are part of the case.

Telegraph Road (US-24).

A seven- and eight-lane divided highway through both halves of the city, from Van Born in the south to Joy Road in the north, with a stretch through Dearborn between them. It carries tractor-trailers between I-94, just south of the city in Taylor, and the industrial areas and freeways to the north.

c.v: Warren Avenue, the county roads, and the neighborhoods.

Warren, Joy, Van Born, Cherry Hill, Beech Daly, Inkster, and Outer Drive carry delivery trucks, construction trucks, garbage trucks, and school buses. On Warren, trucks supply the restaurants, bakeries, and markets of the north end.

In 2024, according to the Michigan State Police, 3,916 heavy trucks and buses were involved in crashes in Wayne County, compared with 2,081 in Oakland County and 1,257 in Macomb. Statewide, 110 people were killed and 3,613 injured in heavy truck and bus crashes. Dearborn Heights recorded 1,251 crashes of all kinds, 268 of them on U.S. routes (Telegraph and Michigan Avenue) and 288 on a state route (Ford Road).

sections.heading: Where Dearborn Heights truck crashes happen

c.v: Telegraph Road.
Tractor-trailers share eight lanes with retail and apartment traffic, through signals at Van Born, Annapolis, Michigan Avenue, Ford, Warren, and Joy. The crashes are:

items.v: rear-end and underride crashes at the signals, where a loaded truck needs far more distance to stop
lane changes into a car in the blind spot on the right side of the cab
wide right turns onto the cross streets and into driveways that catch a car on the inside of the turn
trucks making U-turns at the median crossovers, across the opposing lanes

c.v: A car that strikes the side or rear of a trailer can go under it. That is an
underride

crash, which is often fatal or catastrophic. Trailers must carry rear impact guards that meet federal standards (49 CFR 393.86). A missing, damaged, or substandard guard is evidence against the carrier and the trailer’s owner.
Michigan Avenue.
US-12 carries tractor-trailers, flatbeds, and car haulers across the middle of the city, past industrial and commercial frontage and the 20th District Court. The crashes are:

items.v: wide turns into industrial and commercial driveways
slow left turns across oncoming lanes into a plant, yard, or lot
trucks pulling out of a driveway into traffic that cannot stop
rear-end crashes at the Telegraph and Inkster signals
trucks parked or staged on the shoulder without warning devices (49 CFR 392.22)

c.v: On designated Michigan routes, heavy trucks can weigh up to 164,000 pounds, about twice the federal Interstate limit. When a site’s driveway design or truck-staging practice puts trucks in the road, the site’s operator or owner can share responsibility with the carrier.
Ford Road and the retail strips.
Box trucks, beverage trucks, and tractor-trailers supply the stores and restaurants along Ford Road and Telegraph. The crashes are:

items.v: wide right turns into a strip-center driveway
trucks backing into and out of loading areas and service drives
trucks stopped in a lane for a delivery
pedestrians struck by a truck in a parking lot

c.v: Warren Avenue deliveries.
Warren’s restaurants, bakeries, and markets are supplied by box trucks and vans that often stop at the curb or in a travel lane on a street with heavy foot traffic. The crashes are:

items.v: cars striking a truck stopped in the lane, or swerving into another lane to get around it
pedestrians stepping out from behind a stopped truck
trucks backing into an alley or lot without a spotter

c.v: Where a business’s delivery arrangements routinely put trucks in the street or the lot’s traffic lanes, the business can share responsibility. See our
pedestrian accident page
Apartment complexes, construction, and garbage trucks.

Moving trucks, furniture trucks, and package vans serve the apartment complexes along Telegraph, Ford Road, and Van Born. Construction trucks serve building and road work. Garbage and recycling trucks work the neighborhoods in both halves of the city. The crashes are backing crashes, crashes with vehicles stopped in a lane, and children and pedestrians struck by a truck pulling away. Delivery vans are often operated by contracted delivery companies rather than by the retailer named on the package.
Lost and spilled loads.

Cargo, scrap, gravel, or debris that falls from a truck is a violation of the federal cargo securement rules (49 CFR 393.100 and following) and of Michigan law (MCL 257.720). The carrier and the company that loaded the truck can both be responsible.
Whose road it is.
Dearborn Heights is a city, and the road owner can be any of three agencies:
MDOT

items.v: for Telegraph, Michigan Avenue, and Ford Road. A road-defect claim against the State goes to the Court of Claims, with written notice filed there within 120 days (MCL 691.1404).

c.v: Wayne County

items.v: for Warren and other major roads. Written notice is due within 120 days (MCL 691.1402, 691.1404).

c.v: The City of Dearborn Heights

items.v: for the local streets. Written notice is due within 120 days.

sections.heading: Checking a trucking company’s safety record

c.v: Every interstate carrier, and many Michigan intrastate carriers, has a USDOT number painted on the cab door. That number pulls up the carrier’s federal record:
The FMCSA Company Snapshot

items.v: (on the SAFER website) shows the carrier’s registered name and address, its number of trucks and drivers, and its inspections and crashes over the past two years. Its insurance on file is in FMCSA’s Licensing and Insurance system. The inspection results include the out-of-service rates for its vehicles and drivers.

c.v: The FMCSA Safety Measurement System

items.v: groups the carrier’s inspection and crash results by category, including unsafe driving, hours-of-service compliance, vehicle maintenance, and controlled substances and alcohol. Some category results are not shown to the public.

c.v: The carrier’s safety rating,

items.v: if FMCSA has rated it, is “satisfactory,” “conditional,” or “unsatisfactory.” Many carriers have never been rated.

c.v: A poor record does not by itself prove fault in a crash. It can support a claim that the carrier failed to supervise or maintain its fleet, and that a shipper or broker was negligent in hiring a carrier with that record.

When the truck belongs to an owner-operator leased to a larger carrier, the lease generally makes the carrier responsible for the truck’s operation (49 CFR 376.12). The truck may display the carrier’s name and USDOT number rather than the owner-operator’s. The insurance on file with FMCSA, and the carrier’s own policy, are the first insurance we identify.

sections.heading: Who is responsible, and who pays

c.v: The carrier, not just the driver.

The motor carrier is responsible for its drivers’ compliance with the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Regulations. It is liable for a driver’s negligence in the course of employment. Michigan applies the federal rules to intrastate carriers (MCL 480.11a). A local hauler running between a yard on Michigan Avenue and a plant down the road is held to the same standards as an interstate carrier.
These are the rules that decide truck cases most often:

head.v: What it means for the case

rows.v: 11 hours driving in a 14-hour window after 10 hours off; 60/70-hour weekly limits; recorded on an electronic logging device. Some short-haul drivers are exempt from logs but not from the limits.
CDL, medical certificate, driving record, background check. Negligent hiring and retention are claims against the carrier.
Alcohol within 8 hours and drugs within 32 hours after a fatal crash, or after an injury or tow-away crash with a citation.
Pre-trip inspections, defect reports, maintenance records. Brake, tire, lighting, and reflective-tape cases are maintenance cases.
Loads must be contained or secured so they cannot shift or fall. A spilled load is evidence of a violation.
Equipment: rear impact guards, lighting, reflectors
Underride guards (393.86) and conspicuity marking. A trailer that cannot be seen at night or lacks a working guard is a defective trailer.
Warning devices for a stopped truck; reduce speed or stop in snow, ice, and fog; no handheld phone use.
$750,000 general freight; $1 million oil; $5 million hazardous materials.
The lease between an owner-operator and a carrier, and the carrier’s responsibility for the leased truck.

c.v: The owner of the truck or trailer.

In Michigan, a vehicle’s owner is liable for its negligent operation by someone driving with the owner’s consent (MCL 257.401). When the tractor, the trailer, and the driver belong to different companies, each may be a defendant, although a company in the business of renting or leasing vehicles is generally shielded from owner liability by federal law (49 USC 30106).
Michigan no-fault still applies to you.
Your own auto insurer pays these benefits regardless of fault (MCL 500.3107):

items.v: your medical bills, up to the PIP medical level you chose (MCL 500.3107c)
85 percent of lost wages, up to the monthly cap DIFS sets each year
replacement services
attendant care

c.v: Written notice is due within one year (MCL 500.3145(1)). If you have no household policy, a vehicle occupant claims from the insurer of the vehicle they were in, and then the Assigned Claims Plan (MCL 500.3114(4), 500.3172). A pedestrian or cyclist with no household policy claims through the Assigned Claims Plan (MCL 500.3115).

Your claim against the driver and the carrier is for pain and suffering and for losses beyond no-fault, including medical bills above your PIP level. It requires a threshold injury (MCL 500.3135) and must be filed within three years (MCL 600.5805(2)). Michigan’s comparative fault rule is modified, not pure:
More than 50 percent at fault:

items.v: you cannot recover pain-and-suffering damages.

c.v: 50 percent or less:

items.v: your share reduces them (MCL 500.3135(2)(b); MCL 600.2959). At exactly 50 percent, you recover half.

c.v: The noneconomic damages caps apply to medical malpractice and to product liability claims, such as a claim against the maker of a failed part (MCL 600.1483, 600.2946a), not to the claim against the driver and carrier.

The difference from a car case is the money available: the carrier’s $750,000-plus policy, often with excess coverage above it. If the carrier’s coverage still falls short, your own underinsured motorist coverage may add to it. Your insurer’s written consent is needed before you accept the carrier’s limit. See our

items.v: for a government truck (MDOT, Wayne County, the City of Dearborn Heights, SMART, or a school bus), the agency, under the motor vehicle exception to governmental immunity (MCL 691.1405)

c.v: If you were the truck driver.

Workers’ compensation pays your benefits, and your employer usually cannot be sued (MCL 418.131). If you were injured in your employer’s truck, no-fault benefits generally come from the insurer of that truck (MCL 500.3114(3)). They are coordinated with comp, which is paid first (MCL 500.3109(1)). You can also sue a third party, such as another driver or a business whose dock or yard caused the crash. An owner-operator’s coverage depends on the lease and on whether the driver carries workers’ compensation or occupational accident coverage. See our

sections.heading: The evidence, and how fast it disappears

c.v: Carriers must keep two kinds of records for a limited time:

items.v: hours-of-service records, for six months (49 CFR 395.8)
driver inspection reports, for three months (49 CFR 396.11)

c.v: After that, the regulations no longer require them. Other evidence goes faster:

items.v: store, restaurant, gas-station, and industrial-site cameras along Telegraph, Michigan Avenue, Ford Road, and Warren, and dash cameras, overwrite in days to weeks
the truck’s engine control module and event data recorder can be cleared when the truck is repaired and returned to service
a spilled load is swept up within hours
a damaged rear guard can be replaced before anyone measures it

items.v: the ELD and engine data
dash camera footage
the driver’s qualification file and post-crash test results
dispatch records, bills of lading, gate logs, and delivery records
maintenance files
the lease, if an owner-operator was driving
the truck and trailer themselves, for inspection of the brakes, lights, load securement, and rear guard

c.v: Once a party knows a claim is coming, destroying that evidence exposes it to spoliation sanctions.

faqs.question: How many truck accidents happen in Dearborn Heights?

answer.v: The State’s county profile does not break out truck crashes by city. Countywide, 3,916 heavy trucks and buses were involved in Wayne County crashes in 2024. Statewide, 15,888 crashes involved a heavy truck or bus, and 110 people were killed.

faqs.question: How do I check a trucking company’s safety record?

answer.v: Find the USDOT number on the cab door or in the police report and look it up on the FMCSA’s SAFER website. The Company Snapshot shows the carrier’s inspections, crashes, out-of-service rates, and any safety rating. Its insurance on file is in FMCSA’s Licensing and Insurance system. A poor record is not proof of fault in your crash, but it can matter to claims against the carrier and against a shipper or broker that hired it.

faqs.question: A semi swung wide turning off Telegraph and I hit it. Whose fault is that?

answer.v: It depends on the facts. A truck driver must make a wide turn safely and signal it, and a driver who turns across lanes without checking can be at fault. A driver who passes a truck that is signaling a turn can carry fault too. The trailer’s lights and markings, and the truck’s dash camera, are often the deciding evidence.

faqs.question: A delivery truck was stopped in the lane on Warren and I hit it, or swerved and hit something else. Whose fault is that?

answer.v: It depends. A truck stopped in a travel lane without warning, or where stopping is prohibited, can carry fault, and so can a business whose deliveries routinely put it there. Your own speed and attention matter too.

faqs.question: My car went under the back of a trailer at a Telegraph signal. Is that the truck’s fault?

answer.v: It may be partly or wholly. Trailers must carry rear impact guards built to federal standards. A guard that is missing, bent, or too high to stop a car is evidence against the carrier and the trailer’s owner. The trailer has to be inspected before it is repaired.

faqs.question: Is there a cap on what I can recover from a trucking company?

answer.v: Not on pain and suffering against the driver or carrier. Michigan’s damages caps apply to medical malpractice and product liability claims. In practice, the limit is the insurance available: the carrier’s policy, any excess policy, and your own underinsured coverage.

faqs.question: Why does the lawyer need to act within days?

answer.v: Because the records expire. Hours-of-service logs must be kept for six months and inspection reports for three. Camera footage lasts days or weeks. The truck’s electronic data and the trailer’s damage can disappear when the truck is repaired.
